cues.text: A Vatican Diplomat
Born Giovanni Battista Montini in 1897 near Brescia, Italy, to a lawyer and journalist father active in Catholic political life, the future pope was ordained in 1920.
He joined the Vatican's Secretariat of State in 1924, spending three decades there as one of Pope Pius XII's closest and most trusted advisors.
He was named Archbishop of Milan in 1954 and made a cardinal by John XXIII in 1958.
Elected Mid-Council
Elected pope on 21 June 1963, following the death of John XXIII midway through the Second Vatican Council .
Paul VI immediately committed to continuing the Council his predecessor had begun.
He personally presided over its remaining three sessions and formally closed it on 8 December 1965.
Implementing the Council

The bulk of Paul VI's fifteen-year papacy was devoted to the difficult, often contentious work of implementing the Council's sweeping reforms — a new vernacular liturgy, revised rites for the sacraments, and a reorganized Roman Curia.
Throughout, he attempted to steer a careful course between Catholics urging faster change and those resisting it, a tension that marked his entire pontificate.
A Traveling Pope
Breaking with centuries of papal tradition, Paul VI became the first pope in over 150 years to leave Italy, undertaking apostolic journeys to seventeen countries across five continents.

That included a historic 1964 meeting in the Holy Land with Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I, at which the two leaders mutually lifted the excommunications of 1054 that had formally divided the Catholic and Orthodox Churches for nine centuries.
Humanae Vitae

Paul VI's most consequential and controversial act was the 1968 encyclical Humanae Vitae , in which he reaffirmed the Church's traditional teaching against artificial contraception at a moment when many had expected the teaching to be relaxed.
The intense backlash the document provoked, both within and outside the Church, was so severe that Paul issued no further encyclicals for the remainder of his papacy.
Legacy
Paul VI died at Castel Gandolfo on 6 August 1978, having overseen the most sweeping period of institutional and liturgical change the Catholic Church had experienced in centuries.
Beatified in 2014 and canonized in 2018 by Pope Francis, he is remembered as the pope who carried Vatican II's vision from council chamber into the daily life of the Church.
He steered its implementation through some of the most turbulent years the modern Church has faced.
